items.title: Train, validation, and test splits
items.body: Fit models on the training set, choose hyperparameters and models on the validation set (or with cross-validation), and use the test set once at the end for an unbiased estimate. Tuning against the test set turns it into another validation set.

items.title: A model too good to be true
items.question: Your churn model scores 0.99 AUC offline and is useless in production. You scaled features on the full dataset and split randomly. What happened?
items.answer: Data leakage: fitting the scaler on all rows let test statistics into training, and a random split may put the same customer or future events on both sides. Fit preprocessing inside a Pipeline on training data only, split by time or by group, and drop features unavailable at prediction time.

source.name: scikit-learn - Common pitfalls and recommended practices

items.title: Choosing precision or recall
items.question: A fraud model is 99.5 percent accurate but fraud is 0.5 percent of transactions. How should you evaluate it?
items.answer: Accuracy is meaningless here because predicting never-fraud scores 99.5 percent. Use precision (of flagged, how many are fraud) and recall (of fraud, how many are flagged), a precision-recall curve, and pick a threshold based on the cost of missed fraud versus false alarms.

items.title: Cosine similarity on embeddings
items.body: Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors, ignoring magnitude, with values from -1 to 1. For unit-normalized embeddings it equals the dot product, which is why vector search often normalizes and uses inner product.

items.title: Why training loss falls as validation rises
items.question: Why does validation loss start rising while training loss keeps falling?
items.answer: The model is overfitting: it memorizes noise and specifics of the training data that do not generalize. Remedies include more data, regularization, simpler models, dropout, and early stopping at the validation minimum.

items.title: Gradient descent and learning rate
items.body: Gradient descent updates weights by a step against the gradient of the loss, scaled by the learning rate. Too small and training crawls; too large and loss oscillates or diverges.
items.question: Think: your loss becomes NaN after a few steps. What do you try first?
items.answer: Lower the learning rate (or add warmup and gradient clipping), and check the inputs for unscaled features or bad values.
